query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high‐entropy alloy, high strain rate sliding in an ultra‐high vacuum induces dynamic grain refinement that lowers the grain-boundary cohesion, triggering brittle intergranular decohesion and consequent toughness degradation—even in the absence of conventional segregation or intermetallic precipitation.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially coarse-grained, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi)
generation.intervention: Application of high strain rate sliding in UHV to induce dynamic severe plastic deformation
generation.conditions: Comparison between high strain rate sliding in UHV and a control condition maintained under static (low strain rate) loading at similar temperatures, ensuring no oxidation or significant thermal effects
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic formation of ultrafine/nanocrystalline grains (with high-angle grain boundaries) at the contact surfaces
generation.mechanism: The high strain rate sliding promotes rapid grain refinement below a critical size where dislocation-mediated plasticity is inhibited. As grain boundary sliding becomes dominant, the high-energy, ultrafine grain boundaries exhibit reduced cohesive strength, leading to cavitation or intergranular decohesion that degrades toughness. This mechanism contrasts with conventional alloys where segregation and precipitation govern embrittlement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high strain rate sliding, the alloy will develop a surface layer of nanoscale grains accompanied by intergranular cavitation/decohesion, leading to lower fracture toughness compared to the static condition which retains a coarser microstructure and better ductility.
generation.baseline: The HEA in its as-processed, relatively coarse-grained state maintained under static or low strain rate conditions without significant dynamic grain refinement
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under high strain rate sliding in environments free of reactive species (i.e., UHV) and may not directly extend to conditions with thermal activation or oxidation, where segregation or precipitation could become relevant.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical grain size for the transition and the quantitative impact on toughness degradation are not fully defined; other mechanisms (such as dynamic strain aging) may also contribute under different conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the single-phase HEA. Subject one group to high strain rate sliding in UHV conditions to induce dynamic grain refinement, while maintaining a control group under static (low strain rate) loading conditions. After testing, examine both groups via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for grain size distribution and via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for microstructural evidence of intergranular cavitation/decohesion. Conduct mechanical tests (fracture toughness, tensile ductility) on both groups.
measurements: Grain size distribution from TEM imaging
SEM observations of intergranular decohesion or cavitation
Friction coefficient and wear rate during sliding
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples subjected to high strain rate sliding do not show a statistically significant reduction in grain size, or if no evidence of grain boundary decohesion (e.g., intergranular cavitation) and toughness degradation is observed relative to the static controls, then the hypothesis that dynamic grain refinement drives brittle behavior in the absence of segregation is falsified.

Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Although recent experimental measurements of HAGB energy with this same alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) exist, a comparison of this prediction is difficult. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution. reading.lever: Apply high strain rate sliding in UHV to induce dynamic grain refinement and assess grain boundary decohesion versus static conditions.
reading.why: This approach, validated on a related HEA system, offers a direct test of whether dynamic microstructural evolution, rather than segregation, governs toughness degradation in single‐phase high-entropy alloys.
